build_check.description: index.html and game_logic.js exist, a canvas/WebGL renderer is present, and no disallowed heavy runtime asset references are used.

requirements.description: One-button flight physics work as a playable loop: gravity accelerates the bird downward, each tap applies a consistent upward impulse that resets downward velocity, and repeated taps create controllable arcs. The bird is frozen in a ready hover before first input and only begins falling once the player acts. Score 1 if ready-freeze, gravity pull, upward impulse, and arc control all function in the same run. Score 0 if the bird does not respond to input, teleports, moves on rails, or starts falling before first input.

Endless obstacle spawning produces a continuous corridor: paired top/bottom hazards appear off-screen right at regular intervals, scroll left at constant speed, maintain a uniform gap height, and randomize the gap center within safe bounds. Score 1 if multiple pairs demonstrate fixed spacing, uniform clearance, randomized vertical placement, and continuous scrolling. Score 0 if obstacles are static, single-sided, or stop spawning.

Collision and defeat are accurate: touching a pipe, floor, or ceiling triggers immediate defeat, freezes scrolling and physics, and presents a result state. Score 1 if collision detection, world freeze, and result display all trigger correctly on contact. Score 0 if the bird passes through hazards or defeat occurs without contact.

Scoring increments correctly and retry resets the loop: passing a hazard pair adds exactly one point, the run starts at zero, and a retry control returns to the ready state without relaunching the executable. Score 1 if score increments on pass, resets on retry, and the full loop is replayable. Score 0 if score is decorative or retry requires restarting.

Difficulty progresses over the course of a run: at least two pacing changes are observable such as faster scroll speed, narrower safe margins, shifted pipe cadence, or new hazard behaviors. Score 1 if progression affects survival decisions while preserving fair gaps. Score 0 if every obstacle remains identical forever.

Obstacle variety provides authored content: at least three visually distinct hazard presentations appear across play, such as different pipe styles, plasma gates, moving shutters, or warning zones. They must remain mechanically readable. Score 0 if all hazards are identical rectangles or only one presentation exists.

High-score persistence and record feedback are functional: the best score is saved locally, loaded on the title screen, updated when beaten, and a new-best indicator is shown on the result screen. Score 1 if save/load, new-best detection, and display all work. Score 0 if there is no persistence or high-score system.

Replay-value systems beyond raw score exist: at least one secondary feedback layer such as medals, streak counters, speed-tier labels, run-length stats, or milestone cues is integrated into the loop and visible to the player. Score 0 if the game offers only a single score number with no meta feedback.

Gameplay readability at speed: the bird, safe gap, incoming hazards, floor/ceiling danger, and score are visually distinguishable at 1280x720 during motion without relying on debug labels. Score 1 if a player can judge gap position and bird trajectory precisely. Score 0 if hazards blend into the background or collision boundaries are unclear.

State-change feedback is visible: flap impulse, score increment, defeat collision, world freeze, and retry reset each produce observable visual response. Score 1 if both successful and failed actions are clearly communicated. Score 0 if state changes happen without visible feedback.

HUD and UI text are readable in every game state: title shows high score and start affordance, ready state shows input prompt, gameplay shows current score, result shows final/best score and retry control. All text has sufficient contrast and spacing. Score 0 if core UI is hidden, overlapping, or unreadable.

The game flow connects title -> ready -> flight -> defeat -> result -> retry without requiring an executable restart. Score 1 if the full loop is playable end-to-end in a single session. Score 0 if major transitions are missing or broken.

The game has a coherent dark/cyberpunk art direction: bird, hazards, skyline, HUD, title, and result screens share a consistent palette and visual language that reads as authored rather than assembled from mismatched parts. Score 1 if screenshots read as a publishable vertical slice. Score 0 if visible gameplay relies on raw ColorRect shapes, default HTML 引擎 controls, or generic bright placeholder colors. Full credit may be earned with runtime-authored procedural textures, layered materials, deliberate multi-light rigs, particles, synthesized audio, or post-processing; external asset files are not required.

The bird is recognizable character art with a distinct silhouette, detail beyond a primitive shape, and at least one animation state (flap, bob, or velocity tilt) visible across frames. Score 1 if the avatar could plausibly ship as final art. Score 0 if the bird is a circle, rectangle, or icon-less placeholder.

Hazards and environment have surface detail and atmospheric depth: pipes/gates show texture, glow, or structural detail; the background has parallax layers or depth cues; atmospheric elements like smog, particles, or haze are present. Score 1 if the playfield feels like a world rather than flat bars on a solid fill. Score 0 if hazards are untextured rectangles and the background is a single color.

UI chrome is custom and themed: title, score display, result panel, and retry button use styled fonts, borders, panels, or effects matching the game's visual identity. Score 1 if no primary UI element reads as an unstyled default Label or Button. Score 0 if the UI is mostly naked default widgets or plain floating text.
